analysis.one_liner: Extends expiring ACA premium subsidies two years while restricting who qualifies.
analysis.headline: A one-sponsor bill to extend the expiring ACA premium subsidies through 2027 — with new citizen-only eligibility, a 600%-of-poverty income cap, a $5 minimum premium, and an abortion-coverage ban — has no cosponsors and sits untouched in the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The enhanced tax credits that lower monthly premiums for people who buy their own health insurance through the ACA Marketplaces are set to expire at the end of 2025. This bill would extend them for two more years, through 2027, but with new conditions: only U.S. citizens could receive the credits, subsidies would end for households earning more than six times the poverty level, every enrollee would have to pay at least $5 a month, and plans covering abortion (outside narrow exceptions) could no longer sell subsidized Marketplace coverage. It would also write a permanent, open-ended appropriation for the federal payments that reduce deductibles and copays for lower-income enrollees.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own coverage on the ACA Marketplaces — mostly self-employed workers, small-business employees, and early retirees — would keep their premium subsidies for two more years instead of seeing premiums jump when the enhanced credits lapse after 2025. Health insurers selling Marketplace plans keep a subsidized customer base, and starting in 2027 they would again receive the federal cost-sharing payments that lower deductibles for lower-income enrollees. The restrictions (citizens-only, $5 minimum, income cap, abortion ban) mean fewer people qualify than under current law, so the extension is narrower than simply keeping the status quo.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Marketplace customers and the insurers who cover them

how_it_helps.text: Extends the enhanced ACA premium tax credits through 2027 by moving the expiration date from 2025 to the end of 2027, so premiums for Marketplace customers do not snap back to pre-2021 levels when the enhanced credits lapse after 2025.

Keeps subsidies available up to 600% of the federal poverty level — roughly six times the poverty line — instead of the 400% cap that returns under current law, so upper-middle-income families buying their own coverage keep some help (at a graduated, rising premium share).

Writes an open-ended appropriation — 'such sums as may be necessary' — for the Affordable Care Act's cost-sharing reduction payments beginning in 2027, the federal money that pays insurers to cut deductibles and copays for lower-income enrollees.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through an open-ended appropriation and continued tax-credit outlays; the bill partially offsets that by cutting off subsidies for lawfully present non-citizens and for households above 600% of poverty, and by requiring every enrollee to pay at least $5 a month. Enrollees also pay in kind: Marketplace plans nationwide would lose abortion coverage, and lawfully present immigrants would lose credits they currently receive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, plus immigrants and abortion-coverage patients

drawbacks.text: It cuts off premium tax credits for lawfully present non-citizens — green-card holders and people working in the U.S. on visas — by rewriting the eligibility rule to require U.S. citizenship rather than lawful presence, ending help they receive today.

It bans abortion coverage in the subsidized Marketplaces: any plan that covers abortion (except where the mother's life is endangered or the pregnancy results from rape or incest) cannot be a qualified health plan, so Marketplace customers in most states would lose a benefit many currently have.

It caps eligibility at 600% of the federal poverty level, so the highest earners who qualify under the current enhanced credit would lose subsidies entirely, and it requires a minimum $5 monthly premium, ending the $0-premium plans millions of low-income enrollees have now.

The extension runs only through 2027, recreating the same expiration cliff two years from now rather than settling the policy, and the open-ended cost-sharing appropriation adds to federal deficits without a limit or offset.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The extension prevents a real, immediate premium shock for millions of Marketplace customers, which is its genuine value. But the price is a narrower, more conditional subsidy: it strips credits from lawfully present immigrants, ends help above 600% of poverty, ends $0-premium plans, bans abortion coverage in Marketplace plans, and sets up another expiration fight in 2027. Someone who supports extending the subsidies could fairly object that this design helps fewer people than simply continuing current law, and attaches unrelated policy changes to a deadline-driven extension.

outcome.mechanism: It's a brand-new bill from a single senator that went straight to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and hasn't moved since.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Husted introduced the bill on December 9, 2025, with no cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where it has sat with no markup, no vote, and no further action of any kind.
Meanwhile, under current law the enhanced premium tax credits lapse for taxable years beginning after 2025, so the window the bill is meant to address closes at the end of December 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one. Nothing has been decided; if Congress passes nothing before the credits lapse, Marketplace customers face higher 2026 premiums, while opponents of the enhanced credits are better off with the delay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill hasn't moved

for.name: Sen. Jon Husted
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its only sponsor; it has drawn no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on December 9, 2025; no markup, hearing, or vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred and no other member of either party has cosponsored, so the partisan shape is a single Republican sponsor and nothing else.

industries.note: The extension keeps federal premium subsidies flowing through private Marketplace plans, locking insurers in as the permanent channel for this public help, and the new cost-sharing appropriation would send unlimited federal payments directly to insurers starting in 2027. The bill does regulate what those plans must cover (banning abortion coverage) and trims the eligible pool, but its main effect is preserving insurers' subsidized revenue base.

industries.industry: Abortion providers and reproductive health clinics
industries.note: By disqualifying any plan that covers abortion from the Marketplaces, the bill removes abortion coverage from subsidized insurance everywhere except the narrow life/rape/incest exceptions, cutting off both payment to providers and coverage for the patients who use it.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action, the bill is unlikely to advance on its own. The likelier paths are that it sits in Finance until the Congress ends, or that its provisions — citizen-only eligibility, the $5 minimum premium, the 600% cap, the abortion restriction — get folded into whatever broader deal leadership negotiates over the expiring subsidies. Absent action, the enhanced credits lapse after 2025 and Marketplace premiums rise in 2026.
